summary: Estimation and checking are habits of mind for judging whether an answer is sensible, not extra calculations. Learners round FIRST to get a ballpark, then calculate, then compare; and they check using the inverse operation (adding the answer back to test a subtraction) understood as an independent re-derivation, not a repeat of the same sum. Aimed at ages 7-9 working with sums and differences of two- and three-digit numbers.
misconceptions: Treating estimation as pointless — 'you can't know until you do the real sum'
Estimating AFTER calculating, bending the estimate to match the answer already found (confirmation)
'Checking' by repeating the identical operation (which reproduces the same error) instead of using the inverse
Rounding erratically so the estimate isn't a fair ballpark

activities.title: Sensible or silly? Judge before you compute
steps: Look at a calculation paired with a proposed answer, e.g. 412 + 389 = 121, and decide quickly whether it is 'sensible' or 'silly' BEFORE working out the exact answer
Say aloud the rounded ballpark you used: '400-and-something plus about 390 is roughly 800, so 121 can't be right'
Judge a batch of items, some with reasonable answers (e.g. 801) and some deliberately wrong, flagging the silly ones
Record your estimate and the exact answer side by side in two columns, so you can compare the ballpark against the worked result
Only after committing to your judgement, work out or reveal the exact answer and see whether your estimate caught the nonsense
activities.insight: A rounded ballpark, formed before calculating, is enough to catch a wildly wrong answer — so estimation is a genuine check, not busywork or a guess made after the fact.

activities.title: Check by adding back: the inverse as an independent test
steps: Take a completed subtraction, e.g. 623 − 178 = 445, and check it by adding the answer back: 445 + 178
Confirm that the sum returns to the starting number (623) — if it does, the subtraction is verified
Contrast this with simply redoing 623 − 178 again, and explain why repeating the identical operation can easily repeat the original mistake, while adding back tests the answer a different way
Use a bar model (the whole minus one part returns the other part) and a fact-family triangle linking the three numbers to see how addition and subtraction undo each other
activities.insight: Checking with the inverse operation is an independent re-derivation of the answer, whereas repeating the same subtraction just reproduces the same potential error.

activities.title: How do you KNOW it's right? Reasoning discussion
steps: Respond to a prompt such as: 'A friend adds 412 + 389 and gets 121; another gets 801. Without working out the exact sum, how could you tell which answer must be wrong?'
Explain how to check a subtraction like 623 − 178 WITHOUT just doing the same subtraction again
Discuss: if your estimate and your exact answer disagree, which do you trust, and what do you do next?
Consider whether an answer could be close to the estimate but still wrong — so what does an estimate tell you, and what does it not?
activities.insight: An estimate bounds roughly how big an answer should be and flags gross errors, but it does not guarantee exactness; the inverse gives a separate confirmation. Knowing an answer is sensible is a matter of reasoning, not only recomputation.

activities.title: Rounding to a fair ballpark
steps: Round two- and three-digit numbers to the nearest 10 and the nearest 100, e.g. 412 → 410 (nearest 10) or 400 (nearest 100); 389 → 390 (nearest 10) or 400 (nearest 100); 178 → 180 (nearest 10) or 200 (nearest 100)
Use a number line or rounding scale to see which ten or hundred a number is nearest to
Form an estimate for a sum or difference by rounding each number to the SAME place, e.g. 623 − 178 ≈ 620 − 180 ≈ 440 (both to nearest 10)
Compare estimates formed with consistent rounding against erratic rounding to see why fair, consistent rounding gives a trustworthy ballpark
activities.insight: A reliable estimate depends on rounding each number fairly to the same place; erratic rounding produces a ballpark you can't trust.

checkQuestion: Treat this as a discussion, not a marked task — you want the child's reasoning. Say: 'A friend adds 412 + 389 and gets 121; another gets 801. Without working out the exact sum, how could you tell which answer must be wrong?' Then: 'When someone finishes a subtraction like 623 − 178, how could they check it's right WITHOUT just doing the same subtraction again?'
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning rounds to estimate — about 400 + 390 ≈ 800 — so 121 is obviously wrong and 801 is sensible; and checks the subtraction by adding the answer back to 178 to see if it returns 623 (the inverse), or by estimating 620 − 180 ≈ 440. It treats an answer as unreasonable when it is far from the estimate.
